task_5.title: Support x-gzip response decoding
task_5.description: urllib3 now recognizes the legacy Content-Encoding token x-gzip as equivalent to gzip, so gzip-compressed HTTP response bodies using that header value are automatically decompressed when response decoding is enabled.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that HTTP responses declaring Content-Encoding as x-gzip are decoded the same way as responses declaring gzip, so users do not need to manually disable decoding and decompress the body themselves.

expectation.grounded: urllib3 response decoding must treat the content-encoding token x-gzip as a supported gzip-compatible decoder. APIs such as HTTPResponse.read(decode_content=True) and response paths that consult BaseHTTPResponse.CONTENT_DECODERS should return decompressed response bytes for gzip-compressed bodies labeled with x-gzip, matching the observable behavior already provided for gzip.
expectation.conceptual: A gzipped response should be transparently decompressed even when the server uses the x-gzip content-encoding label instead of gzip.

constraints.grounded: Existing gzip and deflate decoding behavior must remain unchanged, and optional brotli or zstd decoding support must continue to be governed by their existing availability. Unknown or unsupported content-encoding values should not become implicitly accepted beyond the newly supported x-gzip alias.
constraints.conceptual: The change should add compatibility for x-gzip without broadening decoding behavior in unrelated ways or regressing existing supported encodings.

behavior: The response decoder registry now includes x-gzip as a recognized content decoder alongside gzip and deflate.
A decoder lookup for the single content-encoding value x-gzip selects the same gzip decompression behavior used for gzip.
Reading a gzip-compressed response body with decoding enabled returns the decompressed payload when the response header uses x-gzip.
Manual decompression is no longer required solely because a server reports x-gzip instead of gzip.
acceptance_criteria: Given a gzip-compressed HTTP response with Content-Encoding: x-gzip, when the response body is read with content decoding enabled, it should return the decompressed bytes.
Given equivalent gzip-compressed response bodies labeled gzip and x-gzip, when both are read through urllib3's response decoding path, they should produce the same decoded content.
When supported content decoders are inspected through urllib3 response metadata, x-gzip should be listed as a supported decoder.
When responses use existing supported encodings such as gzip or deflate, their decoding behavior should remain unchanged.

task_3.title: Drop Python 3.7 support
task_3.description: The 2.1.0 update removes support for end-of-life Python 3.7 and simplifies compatibility behavior that only existed for older runtimes. Supported environments should use Python versions that provide the expected typing and SSL capabilities, while urllib3 should preserve its SSL behavior for supported CPython and PyPy runtimes.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that urllib3 2.1.0 no longer supports Python 3.7 and that related compatibility paths are removed without regressing SSL and SOCKS behavior on supported Python versions.

expectation.grounded: urllib3 should treat Python 3.7 as unsupported. In `urllib3.util.ssl_`, PyPy detection for the BPO-43522 SSL fix should depend on PyPy runtime version `7.3.8` or newer rather than also checking for Python `3.8` or newer. `create_urllib3_context` should enable `SSLContext.post_handshake_auth` only when certificate verification is required and the SSL context exposes that attribute. In `urllib3.contrib.socks`, SOCKS option typing should rely on the standard-library `typing.TypedDict` available in supported Python versions.
expectation.conceptual: Users must run urllib3 on supported Python versions, and SSL context setup should only enable TLS post-handshake authentication when certificate verification actually requires it. Supported PyPy runtimes should continue to receive the correct SSL reliability classification, and SOCKS proxy support should remain available on supported runtimes.

constraints.grounded: Do not preserve Python 3.7-only fallbacks or version gates. Do not enable `post_handshake_auth` merely because the interpreter version is new enough; require `ssl.CERT_REQUIRED` and an SSL context that supports the attribute. Do not mark PyPy versions older than `7.3.8` as fixed for BPO-43522. Do not change the public SOCKS connection behavior while removing the Python 3.7 typing fallback.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should make the supported runtime boundary explicit while avoiding unrelated behavior changes for supported users. Security-sensitive SSL behavior should remain conservative, and proxy functionality should continue to behave the same on supported platforms.

behavior: Python 3.7 is no longer a supported runtime for urllib3 2.1.0.
PyPy SSL fix detection now considers supported PyPy runtimes fixed when the PyPy runtime version is `7.3.8` or newer, without an additional Python-version requirement.
`create_urllib3_context` enables TLS post-handshake authentication only when certificate verification is required and the context supports the setting.
`create_urllib3_context` no longer enables TLS post-handshake authentication solely because the interpreter is at least Python 3.7.4.
SOCKS proxy option typing now assumes `typing.TypedDict` is present in the standard library, reflecting the supported Python baseline.
acceptance_criteria: Given urllib3 2.1.0, when a user attempts to rely on Python 3.7 compatibility, it should be treated as unsupported by the library.
When PyPy SSL reliability is evaluated on a supported Python runtime with PyPy `7.3.8` or newer, it should be considered fixed for the relevant SSL issue.
When PyPy SSL reliability is evaluated with a PyPy runtime older than `7.3.8`, it should not be considered fixed for the relevant SSL issue.
When an urllib3 SSL context is created with required certificate verification and the SSL context supports post-handshake authentication, post-handshake authentication should be enabled.
When an urllib3 SSL context is created without required certificate verification, post-handshake authentication should not be enabled merely because the runtime supports the attribute.
When SOCKS proxy support is imported on supported Python versions, the SOCKS option typing path should load without requiring a Python 3.7 compatibility fallback.

task_2.title: Remove SecureTransport TLS support
task_2.description: urllib3 2.1.0 removes the deprecated macOS SecureTransport TLS backend. Applications can no longer import or inject SecureTransport as urllib3's TLS implementation, and urllib3 no longer exposes SecureTransport compatibility flags or behavior branches. Supported TLS behavior should continue through the standard OpenSSL-backed SSL stack or other supported backends.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the deprecated SecureTransport TLS backend is no longer supported as an injectable urllib3 TLS implementation, and that urllib3 behaves only according to supported SSL backends.

expectation.grounded: The urllib3.contrib.securetransport module, including inject_into_urllib3() and extract_from_urllib3(), is no longer available. The associated SecureTransport context/socket implementation and _securetransport helper modules are removed. urllib3.util.IS_SECURETRANSPORT and urllib3.util.ssl_.IS_SECURETRANSPORT are no longer exposed, and response-reading behavior for very large reads is determined only by PyOpenSSL usage or the Python runtime version.
expectation.conceptual: Users must not be able to opt urllib3 into Apple's SecureTransport TLS implementation. urllib3 should use its supported TLS stack and should not preserve compatibility flags or behavior branches for the removed backend.

constraints.grounded: Do not leave functional injection, extraction, SecureTransport-backed SSLContext replacement, SecureTransport feature flags, or SecureTransport-specific special cases reachable through urllib3 public APIs. Existing supported TLS behavior, including standard ssl and PyOpenSSL paths, must remain available.
constraints.conceptual: Removing the deprecated backend must not degrade supported TLS usage for normal HTTPS clients, but code depending on the removed backend should fail clearly through normal missing-API or missing-module behavior rather than silently enabling SecureTransport.

behavior: Importing urllib3.contrib.securetransport no longer provides a module that can be used to configure urllib3's TLS backend.
inject_into_urllib3() and extract_from_urllib3() no longer exist as supported ways to replace or restore urllib3's SSLContext implementation.
urllib3 no longer exposes IS_SECURETRANSPORT from urllib3.util or urllib3.util.ssl_.
urllib3 no longer maintains a SecureTransport-specific SSL context, wrapped socket, certificate handling, ALPN handling, TLS protocol mapping, or ctypes bindings for macOS Security/CoreFoundation.
Large response read handling no longer has a SecureTransport exclusion; it follows the remaining supported-backend conditions.
acceptance_criteria: When application code attempts to import or use urllib3.contrib.securetransport, it should not be able to enable a SecureTransport-backed TLS implementation.
When application code inspects urllib3.util or urllib3.util.ssl_, it should not find an IS_SECURETRANSPORT compatibility flag.
When urllib3 creates HTTPS connections without SecureTransport, it should continue to use supported SSL behavior through the standard SSLContext or supported injected backend.
When reading a very large HTTP response, urllib3 should apply its large-read safeguards based on PyOpenSSL or the Python runtime version without checking for SecureTransport.

When code relied on SecureTransport-only behavior such as custom SecureTransport socket wrapping, SecureTransport certificate handling, or SecureTransport-specific TLS version support, those behaviors should no longer be part of urllib3's runtime contract.

task_4.title: Support in-memory CA data for proxies
task_4.description: The 2.1.0 update fixes proxy SSL configuration so CA certificate data supplied from memory is accepted for proxy-based connections. This brings proxy handling in line with existing certificate-file behavior and prevents in-memory CA data from being treated as an invalid or unkeyed SSL option.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that proxy-based urllib3 connections can be configured with CA certificates supplied directly from memory, not only from certificate files.

expectation.grounded: Proxy-related pool manager entry points such as proxy_from_url and ProxyManager must accept ca_cert_data as a valid SSL configuration option. The value may be text, bytes, or absent, and it must be represented in PoolKey as key_ca_cert_data so that connection pool identity reflects the configured in-memory CA data.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to provide trusted CA certificate contents directly when configuring a proxy, and requests through that proxy should use the supplied trust material without rejecting the option.

constraints.grounded: Existing SSL keyword behavior for cert_file, cert_reqs, ca_certs, ssl_version, TLS version bounds, and related pool-key fields must remain unchanged. Supplying ca_cert_data must not collapse pools that use different in-memory CA data, and omitting it must continue to behave as before.
constraints.conceptual: The change should only add support for in-memory CA certificate data in proxy configurations and should not weaken existing certificate validation or alter unrelated SSL options.

behavior: ca_cert_data is treated as a recognized SSL keyword during proxy pool manager configuration.
Pool keys include the configured ca_cert_data value as key_ca_cert_data, allowing pool reuse decisions to account for in-memory CA trust material.
Proxy configurations that provide CA certificate data from memory no longer fail because the corresponding pool key field is missing.
Both text and byte-form CA certificate data are valid values for the proxy pool key field, while absence of the option remains supported.
acceptance_criteria: Given a proxy manager is created with ca_cert_data containing CA certificate contents, when requests are made through the proxy, it should accept the option as part of SSL configuration instead of rejecting it as unexpected.
When ca_cert_data is supplied for a proxy configuration, the resulting connection pool identity should include that value so distinct CA data produces distinct pool configuration state.
When ca_cert_data is omitted from a proxy configuration, existing proxy connection behavior should remain unchanged.
When other supported SSL options are supplied to proxy configuration, their existing behavior should continue to work alongside ca_cert_data.

task_1.title: Remove deprecated secure extra support
task_1.description: urllib3 2.1.0 removes support for the deprecated urllib3[secure] extra because supported Python and OpenSSL environments no longer need a separate secure extra for TLS behavior. The runtime also stops performing special import-time handling for the legacy secure-extra marker package, while retaining existing OpenSSL compatibility enforcement.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that urllib3 2.1.0 treats the deprecated urllib3[secure] extra as removed and no longer presents it as a supported way to obtain TLS-related behavior or dependencies.

expectation.grounded: The urllib3[secure] extra must no longer be supported as a meaningful dependency extra in urllib3 2.1.0. Importing urllib3 must not emit a DeprecationWarning solely because the legacy urllib3-secure-extra marker package is installed. Existing SSL compatibility behavior must remain: non-OpenSSL ssl builds warn with urllib3.exceptions.NotOpenSSLWarning, and OpenSSL versions below 1.1.1 raise ImportError, with user-facing wording applying to urllib3 v2 generally.
expectation.conceptual: Users should install and depend on plain urllib3 instead of the old secure extra. The library should not imply that the removed extra provides additional security, and its normal TLS compatibility checks should continue to behave consistently.

constraints.grounded: Do not reintroduce import-time deprecation handling tied to urllib3-secure-extra. Do not weaken the OpenSSL 1.1.1+ requirement or the warning behavior for non-OpenSSL ssl implementations. Do not expand this change into removal of unrelated contrib modules or TLS APIs.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should remove only the obsolete secure-extra contract while preserving existing TLS safety boundaries and unrelated public behavior.

behavior: urllib3[secure] is no longer a supported extra that users or downstream packages should rely on for TLS dependencies or enhanced security behavior.
The presence of the legacy urllib3-secure-extra package no longer causes urllib3 import to emit a secure-extra deprecation warning.
Plain urllib3 remains the supported installation target for modern supported environments.
Import-time SSL compatibility enforcement remains in place for unsupported ssl backends and OpenSSL versions below 1.1.1.
OpenSSL compatibility diagnostics refer to urllib3 v2 as a whole rather than being limited to urllib3 v2.0.
acceptance_criteria: When a user upgrades to urllib3 2.1.0, they should no longer be directed to use urllib3[secure] for additional TLS security behavior.
When the legacy secure-extra marker package is installed, importing urllib3 should not produce a DeprecationWarning solely due to that package.
When urllib3 is imported with an ssl module that is not backed by OpenSSL, it should still emit the existing NotOpenSSLWarning signal.
When urllib3 is imported with OpenSSL older than 1.1.1, it should still fail with ImportError.
When users or downstream packages require pyOpenSSL, certifi, idna, or similar dependencies independently, those dependencies should be handled directly rather than through urllib3[secure].
